h1: SEO for wellness brands making claims they can actually prove
metaTitle: SEO for Wellness Brands: Claims That Survive
metaDescription: SEO for wellness brands in India. We build supplement, therapy and programme content that meets YMYL standards and stays inside FSSAI claim rules.
answer: Wellness brands lose search visibility for one reason: the claim that converts is the claim FSSAI's 2018 advertising rules prohibit. A food or supplement cannot say it treats, prevents or cures anything. So the content has to win on mechanism, dosage, timeline and cited evidence instead — which is also what Google rewards.
takeaways: You sell a food, not a drug. Under the **FSS (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018** a food cannot claim to prevent, treat or cure a disease, and "boosts immunity" is a nutrient function claim with conditions attached, not a slogan.
"Source of" and "high in" are numbers from a schedule, not adjectives. So are `natural`, `pure` and `fresh` — the 2018 regulations set conditions on each of those words.
Health content is **YMYL**. A named, credentialled reviewer and a citation to the actual paper beat a thousand words of confident copy.
Retention content — how long it takes to work, what to take it with, what happens if you stop — ranks *and* keeps the subscription alive. Most brands never write it.
If you run studios or consults as well as products, that's two SEO problems on one domain: a national commerce site and a set of local listings.

sections.h2: The claim that converts is the claim you're not allowed to make
body: Every wellness founder asks some version of the same question: why can't we just say it works? Because your product is licensed as a food, and Indian food law draws a hard line between food and drug. The Food Safety and Standards (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018 prohibit any claim that a food prevents, treats, alleviates or cures a disease, and any claim implying your health will suffer without it. Your label already says "not for medicinal use". A cure-flavoured landing page contradicts your own packaging.

It's also a ranking problem. Google treats health queries as Your Money or Your Life and holds them to a higher evidence bar, so the page that overclaims is the page a hospital outranks. Law and algorithm point the same way here, which is rare enough to be worth using.

callout.title: The disclaimer doesn't rescue the claim
callout.body: A grey six-point "these statements have not been evaluated" line at the bottom of the page does not neutralise a headline promising a cure. Under India's misleading-advertisement guidelines a disclaimer cannot contradict or hide the main claim. If the disclaimer is doing the compliance work, the headline is the problem.

sections.h2: Condition content, written without practising medicine
body: Your buyers don't search for your product. They search for their problem: `supplement for hair fall`, `magnesium for sleep`, `best protein for women over 40`, `why am I always bloated`. That's where the volume is, and it's where most brands either chicken out and publish nothing, or overreach and publish a symptom-checker they have no business publishing.

There's a third page and it beats both. It answers the search honestly, explains the mechanism, gives the ranges used in research, states who it isn't for, and says when to see a doctor instead of buying anything.
numbered: **What's actually going on**, in plain language — the physiology, not a scare paragraph.
**How it's diagnosed**, including the blood test to get before self-medicating. Sending a reader to a lab costs you a sale and buys you a customer who stays.
**What the ingredient does**, at what dose, over what period. "Most trials run 8–12 weeks" beats "fast results", and it sets an expectation you can meet.
**Who should not take it** — pregnancy, thyroid medication, blood thinners. The strongest trust signal available to you, and it costs one paragraph.
**When this isn't a supplement problem.** The brand that tells someone to see a doctor is the brand they come back to.

subs.h3: The internal linking that makes it commercial
body: Condition articles don't need to sell. They need to route. One link to the product, one to the ingredient page, one to the dosage guide — placed after you've answered the question, not before. Structure it as a cluster: an ingredient pillar with condition articles hanging off it, all linking back. The discipline we describe for [healthcare content under Google's YMYL bar](/seo-for/healthcare) applies here, with the extra burden that you're also selling the thing.

sections.h2: Evidence, cited properly, with a name attached
body: "Studies show" is the phrase that tells a search quality rater — and an increasingly literate reader — that no study was read. Wellness is one of the few categories where doing the boring version is a real competitive edge, because so few Indian brands bother. The mechanics take an afternoon per page.
bullets: **A named author with a real credential** — a registered dietitian, an MSc in nutrition, a doctor with a registration number. Not "Team Wellness".

**A named reviewer, separate from the author**, with the review date on the page. Google's [E-E-A-T](/glossary/e-e-a-t) guidance is about demonstrated expertise, and an anonymous byline demonstrates nothing.
**Links to the actual papers**, not to a listicle that linked to one. If the evidence is a single small trial, say so.
**A stated position where evidence is thin.** "Traditionally used for this; the clinical evidence is limited" never loses you a customer and regularly wins you a citation.

callout.title: It also decides whether AI assistants quote you
callout.body: Language models and AI answer panels lean heavily on content with clear attribution, dates and sources when the topic is health. Anonymous, undated, uncited copy is the first thing they discard. The citation habit is doing double duty.

sections.h2: Refill and retention content: the SEO that pays twice
body: Wellness economics are subscription economics. The first order rarely pays for the acquisition; the third one does. So the content that keeps someone taking the product is worth as much as the content that sold it — and people search for it.

`how long does ashwagandha take to work`, `can I take collagen with coffee`, `what happens if I stop taking biotin`. Post-purchase questions with real volume, also read by people still deciding. One page serves a customer and captures a buyer. Most brands publish neither, then wonder why month-two churn is what it is.

subs.h3: Don't wreck it at the cart
bullets: India's dark patterns guidelines, notified in 2023, name **subscription trap**, **basket sneaking**, **false urgency** and **drip pricing** among thirteen listed practices. The auto-added subscription and the countdown that resets on refresh are now a regulatory exposure, not just bad manners.

They're also crutches masking a weak product page. Fix the page: dosage, timeline, what week one feels like, cancellation in one click — a visible cancellation policy tends to raise subscription take-up rather than lower it.

sections.h2: Studios, clinics and consults — the local half of the business
body: Plenty of wellness brands aren't only a bottle. Yoga studios, physiotherapy, nutrition consults, wellness centres — these are local search problems and they behave nothing like the commerce site.

`yoga classes near me`, `nutritionist in indiranagar` are proximity-driven. The Google Business Profile does most of the work, the website supports it, and a national blog does almost nothing for them. If you run both models on one domain, keep them architecturally separate — a commerce tree and a locations tree — so the studio pages aren't buried under 200 ingredient articles.
bullets: **One profile per physical location**, each pointing at its own page — never the homepage.
**A live timetable on the page.** Class times are the query. A PDF from last quarter is not a timetable.
**Trial class or first consult, priced.** "Book a free consultation" converts worse than "first session ₹500, 45 minutes, no card needed".

**Practitioner pages** with real qualifications and registration details. Nutrition and physiotherapy both carry a lot of unqualified practice — being explicit about yours is a differentiator you're currently hiding.

callout.title: The honest timeline
callout.body: Ingredient and condition clusters take three to six months to compound, because they need internal links and citations to mature. Local studio listings move faster — often four to eight weeks. Anyone promising both in month one is planning to buy links and hand you the bill later.

faqs.q: Can a supplement brand in India say its product cures anything?
faqs.a: No. Food and health supplement claims are governed by the FSS (Advertising and Claims) Regulations, 2018, which prohibit claiming that a food prevents, treats, alleviates or cures a disease. Nutrient function claims are allowed if the nutrient is genuinely present at a qualifying level and the claim is substantiated.

faqs.q: Is a disclaimer enough to make a strong wellness claim safe?
faqs.a: No. Under India's misleading-advertisement guidelines a disclaimer cannot contradict the main claim or hide material information. If the headline promises a result the evidence doesn't support, a footnote doesn't fix it — and Google's quality raters treat the same pattern as a reason to demote the page.

faqs.q: Do wellness articles need a medical reviewer?
faqs.a: For anything touching a condition, dose or interaction, yes. Health content sits in Google's Your Money or Your Life category, where demonstrated expertise carries real weight. A named author, a separately named reviewer with credentials, and a visible review date are the minimum. Anonymous health copy competes badly and always will.

faqs.q: How long does SEO take to work for a supplement brand?
faqs.a: Three to six months for ingredient and condition clusters to compound, longer in crowded categories like protein or hair. Product pages for your own branded SKUs move sooner. If you also run studios or clinics, the local listings usually show movement inside four to eight weeks, which is the fastest surface you have.

faqs.q: Should a wellness brand invest in SEO or Instagram first?
faqs.a: In this category they aren't alternatives. Instagram creates the demand and the brand search; SEO catches the research that happens afterwards, when someone checks whether the ingredient actually does what the reel said. Brands that run only one of the two usually pay for the same customer twice.

faqs.q: Can we write about a condition without breaking FSSAI rules?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's the most valuable content you can publish. Explain the physiology, the diagnosis, what the ingredient does at what dose over what period, and who shouldn't take it. What you can't do is connect that education to a promise that your product treats or cures the condition.
